PROJECT NO. 58481
COMMENTS of basf cORPORATION

COMMENTS
BASF appreciates Commission staff’s proposed Discussion Draft that aims to incorporate stakeholder feedback to establish a clear interconnection process and set financial obligations for large loads, as directed by Senate Bill (SB) 6.  BASF would like to take this opportunity to submit comments specifically in response to the new proposed §25.194(l) in the recent draft rule, which provides as follows:
(l)	ERCOT operational standards. 
ERCOT may establish operational standards for large load customers to ensure system reliability.
A large load customer must comply with operational standards, developed through ERCOT protocols, as a condition for interconnection and continued operation of the customer' s load.
At BASF, we create chemistry for a sustainable future. BASF is a diverse global manufacturing and research and development company with an established footprint in Texas. BASF maintains seven distinct manufacturing sites across the state, including five in the ERCOT region (Freeport, Bishop, Pasadena, Caldwell, and Houston), as well as multiple R&D sites, and a large office park in Houston’s Energy Corridor. Additionally, BASF maintains two manufacturing sites outside of ERCOT located in Beaumont and Port Arthur. As a large manufacturer in the state, BASF utilizes a significant amount of electricity by means of purchasing electricity on the retail market, generating our own energy through on-site cogeneration, and by way of engaging in numerous power purchase agreements. 
BASF has operated in Texas since 1958 with the founding of the Freeport, Texas site, which is the second largest industrial complex owned by BASF in the U.S. It is known as a Verbund site, meaning we intelligently connect our production plants and technologies to efficiently use resources and leverage our expertise, ultimately leading to the consumption of less energy. Freeport operates a cogeneration plant that produces electricity and steam necessary for the site’s manufacturing processes. This site does not, however, participate in the wholesale market, but rather remains a retail customer within ERCOT and participates through our TDSP.  
BASF therefore has serious concerns with the proposal that would give ERCOT the authority to impose operational standards on large industrial facilities such as the BASF Freeport site or any future BASF site designated as a large load under these new regulations. First, we don’t believe this drastic regulatory change is necessary to shore up any reliability concerns and therefore ask ERCOT to first show what has changed to necessitate this rule proposal. This would significantly modify the relationship loads have with their utilities, who are better suited to understand the needs and operational requirements of industrial sites.   
Second, ERCOT does not have the expertise to appropriately and safely impose operational restrictions on complex industrial facilities like those that BASF operates, particularly a Verbund site such as Freeport. Operational changes, such as production speed and level, are intricately intertwined and require a great deal of planning and coordination to ensure safe operations. Furthermore, every industrial plant operates uniquely based on their individual production lines and characteristics, which can change based on market responses. We do not believe ERCOT would be best suited to impose any operational restrictions without significant dialogue and further specificity. These system disruptions could create unsafe operating conditions that run contra to the numerous other regulatory regimes chemical plants are subject to (e.g., state and federal environmental regulations, occupational and process safety regulations). 
Any disruptions could also have an adverse economic impact by creating a detrimental domino effect on the production of interconnected facilities. For instance, when one facility is mandated to turn down, it impacts the delivery of product that is slated to go to another plant to safely or economically run their facility, and so on. Therefore, this level of regulatory control would require a substantial amount of internal coordination, as well as a high level of external coordination amongst industrial facilities along the value chain to ensure minimal disruptions to production in a safe manner. Impacts to production in this manner could also negatively impact the financial performance of multinational companies. While we support the need to ensure the functioning of a reliable grid, we are concerned this action is not necessary to achieve that end and could in turn cause considerable economic harm. 
Further, this type of regulatory overreach could adversely impact economic development in the ERCOT region, as it would represent another significant layer of regulation that could effectively disrupt operations and would require significantly more administrative coordination and effort that is not required in other markets.  The added regulatory burden and threat of potential disconnection or substantial operational disruption could therefore hinder the siting of new large operations or expansion of existing assets in the state.  Industrial facilities are accustomed to working directly with their utilities, who have a better understanding of our operations, as well as an incentive to balance reliability with economic viability and growth.  
Finally, this proposed regulatory change was not part of Senate Bill 6, which is the purpose and underpinning of this proposed rule package. Therefore, if this particular proposal were to move forward, we believe it should be undertaken as a standalone proposal to obtain its due attention. We therefore recommend PUC removes this provision. 
We appreciate the opportunity to provide feedback and are open to further discussion. 

Respectfully submitted,

Brad Morrison
SVP, Freeport Site General Manager
BASF Corporation
602 Copper Road
Freeport, TX 77541


PROJECT NO. 58481

BASF’S COMMENTS
Executive Summary
BASF recommends removing proposed §25.194(l) from the draft rule. 
BASF has operated in Texas for decades and has never been subject to operational standards imposed by ERCOT. 
ERCOT does not have the expertise to impose operational standards on large industrial facilities. 
Operational disruptions could create safety and environmental risks and cause economic harm. 
These proposed changes could adversely impact economic development in the state. 
The proposal was not a part of Senate Bill 6 and should be considered separately, if at all.
